meta.audience: The church in the city of Gideon

world_behind.title: There is a town here now
world_behind.text: Four chapters ago this was a valley where an army pitched tents for a night after a battle. The previous chapter reports a city built in it, carrying the same name. Alma is preaching to a congregation that has grown up on ground the record first described as a campsite.

world_behind.title: The visit is only possible because he resigned
world_behind.text: Verse 2 says he could not have come now either, were it not that the judgment-seat has been given to another to reign in his stead. Alma 4 recorded the handover; this verse is the first thing it bought.

world_behind.title: Gideon is the good case, and the record almost never gives one
world_behind.text: Nearly every sermon in this book is addressed to people in trouble. This congregation is not, and the whole first third of the chapter is Alma working out how to speak to people he cannot accuse.

world_behind.title: He speaks in the language of trust
world_behind.text: Verse 6 repeats "I trust" four times in a single line: about pride, about riches, about idols. The negative claims are made about them by someone declining to assert them as facts.

world_behind.title: The birth prophecy is unusually specific
world_behind.text: Verse 10 names the mother, the place, her virginity, the overshadowing, and the child. Most prophecies of the birth in this record give far less; this one reads like an announcement.

world_behind.title: "Jerusalem which is the land of our forefathers."
world_behind.text: The verse glosses its own place name, and the gloss says land rather than city. The phrase occurs once in scripture, and the record is being careful about a distinction that matters to people who left the region six centuries ago.

world_behind.title: The chapter ends as a benediction, and the benediction is material
world_behind.text: The last sentence of a doctrinal sermon is a blessing pronounced over real estate and livestock, and the phrase "from this time forth and forever" is attached to it. Nothing about the ending is abstract.

words.text: Asking humbly, entreating. The participle is unique in scripture and what it governs is unusual: they had continued in the supplicating of his grace. Grace is being asked for repeatedly, which makes it something a congregation stays at instead of arriving at.

A tent, a dwelling meant to be taken down. Treated at 2 Nephi 14:6. "His mortal tabernacle" has no other occurrence in scripture, and Alma uses it in the middle of the one admission he makes about the limits of what he was told. The word holds a body and a temporary structure in the same figure.

Covered by a shadow, in the sense of being enveloped. It is the verb Gabriel used at the annunciation, and it appears five times in this record and three in the New Testament. Here it is passive and Mary is its subject, which puts the action entirely on the other side.

Weaknesses of body and will. Treated at Mosiah 2:11. The verse uses the word twice: he takes them on, and then he knows how to succor his people according to them. The New Testament uses it a dozen times, most memorably of a high priest who can be touched with the feeling of ours.

Bent out of line. The word appears once in this record and the verse uses it of paths God cannot walk in. Three verses earlier the congregation was described as making his paths straight, so the same image is being run from both ends within a single passage.

Holding to a measure, not going to excess. The adjective appears twice in this record and three times in the New Testament, always in a list. Here it sits between long-suffering and diligence, which places moderation among the virtues that require sustained effort.

Without a mark on it. Treated at 2 Nephi 33:7. The word runs eleven times through this record and never appears in the King James Bible. Alma uses it three times in one verse: keep your garments spotless, garments spotless as theirs are spotless. The repetition makes the standard a comparison.

phrases.term: It is the first time that I have spoken unto you by the words of my mouth
phrases.text: An admission placed before anything else. He has been their high priest for nine years and has never preached to them. The clause that follows gives the reason without softening it: he was wholly confined to the judgment-seat, and had much business.

phrases.term: The awful dilemma that our brethren were in at Zarahemla
phrases.text: The word "dilemma" appears twice in scripture and both are in this chapter. It is a word for being caught between options. It is a diagnosis rather than a verdict, and it is applied to the congregation he has just spent a chapter confronting.

phrases.term: My joy cometh over them after wading through much affliction and sorrow
phrases.text: He does not want joy over Gideon on those terms. The figure is of walking through water, slowly, with resistance, and it describes the cost of the previous chapter to the man who wrote it. He is asking this congregation to spare him a repeat.

phrases.term: Now as to this thing I do not know
phrases.text: Six words that change the standing of everything around them. He has just declined to say that Christ will come among his people during the mortal ministry, because the Spirit has not told him. A man about to prophesy in detail first draws a boundary around his own source.

The purpose clause, and it makes the Atonement an education. He takes on infirmities so that he will know. Not so that a price is paid, in this sentence, but so that knowledge is acquired in the only way that kind of knowledge can be. The verb "succor" means to run to someone under a load.

phrases.term: Lay aside every sin, which easily doth beset you
phrases.text: Paul's runner, stripping before a race. The Hebrews passage has weight and sin both laid aside and a race run with patience; here the same figure is attached to walking into the water of baptism. Sin is described as clinging rather than as chosen.

phrases.term: Neither hath he a shadow of turning
phrases.text: James says the Father of lights has no variableness, neither shadow of turning. Alma sets the same phrase inside a longer argument about paths: he cannot walk crooked, does not vary, does not turn right or left. Then he lands it on "his course is one eternal round."

phrases.term: May the peace of God rest upon you, and upon your houses and lands
phrases.text: A blessing that names property. The list runs on through flocks and herds and all that you possess, and only then to your women and your children. It is the shape of a blessing pronounced over an actual farm by someone who is about to leave.

verses.label: v. 1–2
verses.title: A sermon that opens with an administrative fact
verses.text: Before any doctrine the record supplies the reason the speaker is standing there: "even I could not have come now at this time were it not that the judgment-seat hath been given to another, to reign in my stead." The visit is possible because of a resignation reported six chapters earlier, at Alma 4:16–20. The first thing a reader learns in this chapter is not a message but a change of office, and the same verse adds what he did keep, "the Lord in much mercy hath granted that I should come unto you."

verses.label: v. 8–9
verses.title: A prophet marking what he has not been told
verses.text: The record draws a line through the middle of the prediction. First the disclaimer: "I do not say that he will come among us at the time of his dwelling in his mortal tabernacle; for behold, the Spirit hath not said unto me that this should be the case." Then what was said, given as a quotation with its own imperative inside: "the Spirit hath said this much unto me, saying: Cry unto this people, saying, Repent ye, and prepare the way of the Lord." The limit is stated before the message, and the message turns out to be an instruction to deliver a message.

verses.label: v. 10
verses.title: A birthplace, with a gloss that widens it
verses.text: The verse names the mother and the place and then adds four words that change the second: "he shall be born of Mary, at Jerusalem which is the land of our forefathers." The gloss makes Jerusalem a region rather than a city, which is what the phrase land of does everywhere else in the volume. Whether or not the qualifier was needed for the audience, the record supplies it in the same breath as the name, and does not return to the point.

verses.label: v. 17–20
verses.title: A verb repeated until it becomes the argument
verses.text: I perceive opens four clauses in verses 19 and 20, and verse 17 has already set up the method: "do you believe these things? Behold, I say unto you, yea, I know that ye believe them; and the way that I know that ye believe them is by the manifestation of the Spirit which is in me." The speaker asks a question, answers it for the audience, and then states how he is entitled to. What follows is not evidence but repeated assertion of perception, and the record keeps all four instances.

verses.label: v. 23–24
verses.title: A list of qualities with no actions in it
verses.text: The instruction runs as a chain of adjectives and states: "be humble, and be submissive and gentle; easy to be entreated; full of patience and long-suffering; being temperate in all things; being diligent in keeping the commandments of God at all times; asking for whatsoever things ye stand in need." Then verse 24 adds three nouns and one consequence: "faith, hope, and charity, and then ye will always abound in good works." Nothing in the passage tells anyone to do a particular thing. The whole of it describes a disposition and leaves the works to follow from it.

verses.label: v. 27
verses.title: A blessing itemised, ending on people
verses.text: The last verse spreads the blessing over a list instead of pronouncing it generally: "may the peace of God rest upon you, and upon your houses and lands, and upon your flocks and herds, and all that you possess, your women and your children." Houses, land, animals and goods come first, and the women and children come last, after the phrase that would have closed the list. The order is the order of an inventory, and the record ends the sermon on it.

chapter.title: This is the Zarahemla sermon with the accusations taken out
chapter.text: Alma 5 puts its calls as questions, more than forty of them, including "have ye spiritually been born of God?" at verse 14. This chapter puts the same content as statements of perception: "I perceive that ye are in the paths of righteousness" and "I perceive that ye are making his paths straight" at verse 19, and "I perceive that it has been made known unto you" at verse 20. The doctrine is unchanged; verse 14 still says "ye must repent, and be born again." What changes is that the interrogatives of the earlier sermon have become observations about an audience already doing it.

chapter.title: He marks the edge of what he was given
chapter.text: Verse 8 refuses a question about the mortal ministry on the ground that the Spirit has not spoken to it, and then says exactly what the Spirit did say. The refusal sits immediately before the most detailed birth prophecy in the record, and it is what makes the detail worth anything.

chapter.title: The Atonement is described as an education
chapter.text: Verse 12 gives the purpose of taking on infirmities as knowing "according to the flesh how to succor his people." Not only that a debt is settled, but that a competence is acquired, and acquired the hard way, because that knowledge has no other route.

chapter.title: One verb links the doctrine to what a congregation does for the poor
chapter.text: Three chapters earlier the faithful half of the Zarahemla church were succoring those who stood in need of their succor. Here the same verb describes what Christ learned to do by suffering. The sermon puts a congregation's charity and the Atonement under one word.

chapter.title: Every claim is sourced
chapter.text: The Spirit which is in me, the Spirit hath not said, the Spirit hath said this much, this is the testimony which is in me, the testimony of the Holy Spirit which testifieth in me, the manifestation of the Spirit, according to the Spirit which testifieth in me. Seven times in twenty-seven verses he names where a statement came from.

chapter.title: The virtue list is domestic
chapter.text: Nine items, and not one of them will ever be tested by an emergency. There is no courage in the list, no endurance under persecution, no sacrifice. It is a description of how to be in a house on an ordinary day, and it is given to the one congregation in the book that is not in crisis.

chapter.title: The blessing settles on what they own
chapter.text: Houses, lands, flocks, herds, all that you possess, and the women and children come after the livestock in the sentence. Whatever the ordering says about the culture, the record is blessing a working farm town and not an idea.

chapter.title: Role in the book
chapter.text: Alma 7 is the second stop on the circuit and the counterweight to Alma 5. Together they set the range: what to say to a church that has gone wrong, and what to say to one that has not. The next chapter takes him to Melek and then to Ammonihah, where the range runs out.

applications.title: Say plainly why you were absent
applications.text: Nine years, and he opens with the reason and does not dress it up: he had the job, and the job had business. An explanation offered before it is demanded is worth more than one produced under pressure.

applications.title: Speak in trust when you cannot speak from knowledge
applications.text: Four times he says "I trust" rather than "you are." Attributing good to people you cannot verify is a real act, and it is different from flattery because it is marked as an assumption.

applications.title: Say where your information stops
applications.text: He does not know whether Christ will come among his people, and he says so in the middle of a prophecy. Marking the boundary of your knowledge is what makes the inside of it credible.

applications.title: Ask what suffering taught you
applications.text: The verse gives a purpose for the infirmities: so that he would know how to run to people carrying loads. Pain that produced competence is a different thing from pain that was merely endured.

applications.title: Lay it aside
applications.text: The sin easily besets. It clings, like a garment on a runner. Some things are not defeated; they are taken off before you start, and the verse pairs that with a public act on a specific day.

applications.title: Take the ordinary virtues seriously
applications.text: Gentle, patient, easy to be entreated, temperate, thankful. None of these will ever be tested by an emergency. They are what a person is like at home on a Tuesday, and this is the list Alma left with the congregation that was doing well.

applications.title: Bless the actual things
applications.text: Houses, lands, flocks, herds, everything you possess. A blessing that names a person's real property is doing something a general good wish cannot, because it says you looked at what they have.

questions.text: What have I owed someone an explanation for, that I have never simply given?
Whose good outcome do I want, but not at the price it would cost me to get it?
Where could I extend trust to someone instead of waiting for proof?
What am I currently speaking about as if I knew it?
What has my own suffering actually made me able to do for somebody else?
Of the nine things on that list, which would the people who live with me say I am not?
